tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Build a ball-passing network for the Huskies season (one node per player, one link per pass) and characterize its structure and dynamics. Identify dyadic and triadic configurations and the team formation, using multiple spatial scales (pairwise up to all-players) and multiple time scales (minute-to-minute up to the whole game and the whole season). Goal: a quantitative picture of how the 30 Huskies players interact on the ball across 38 matches and 3 coach stints. Scope: Huskies-internal passing (both endpoints Huskies players) from passingevents.csv, joined to matches.csv for context; opponent rows and cross-team passes are used only as context for the turnover analysis in task 2.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) coordinates are on a [0,100]x[0,100] field grid oriented from the attacking team's perspective, so x=100 is the opponent goal; the grid is scaled to a ~210 m pitch, so 1 field unit ~ 2.1 m; (b) a 'pass' row is a completed pass event, and self-passes (147 rows, 0.6%) are retained because a player can receive a pass after a touch; (c) EventTime is seconds within each half, so absolute match time = 2700 s for the second half + EventTime; the maximum observed time (3441 s) includes stoppage time and is accepted as is; (d) with 366 player identities (30 Huskies + 336 opponent) and no substitution table, players are tracked by PlayerID string; substitutions within a match are not separable, which is a limitation for per-player season statistics but not for per-window network structure. Data cleaning (results/data_cleaning_report.json): no duplicates, no missing coordinates in the passing file, no time-order violations after sorting by (MatchID, half, EventTime); 215 full-event rows with missing coordinates were dropped from fullevents.csv; Outcome in matches.csv is 100% consistent with OwnScore vs OpponentScore. Method: a directed, weighted, time-binned network. For each match and each non-overlapping time window (window w in {300, 600, 1200} s, swept), a directed graph G_w is built on the players active in that window with edge weight = pass count. Structural indicators: density, weighted reciprocity (share of directed edges with a return edge), out/in-degree distributions and their Gini coefficients (concentration of contributions), max degree (hub strength), degree assortativity (hub structure), and full enumeration of the 3-node induced subgraphs (triads) classified into the four non-empty directed types (transitive triple, 3-cycle, mutual pair + isolated node, L-shape). Dyads: the top season reciprocal dyads. Scale coverage: pairwise = dyads; meso = triads and hubs; macro = whole-network density/assortativity; time scale = 5-min vs 20-min vs half windows, per-match, per-coach-stint (Coach1: matches 1-9, Coach2: 10-14, Coach3: 15-38) and per 15-minute quarter of the match. This is sound because passing is a directed, repeated, time-embedded interaction: directed edges preserve who drives the play, binning captures the dynamical re-formation the coach asked about, and triad enumeration is the standard micro-meso bridge in social network analysis.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data: P = set of Huskies-internal passes (13,414 of 23,429 total pass rows; OriginTeam=Huskies and DestTeam=Huskies). For match m and window w (seconds), let t_0 be the first pass time in m and I_i = floor((t_i - t_0)/w) the window index. Build G(m,k) = (V, E) where V = players appearing in window k and (u,v) in E with weight n_uv(m,k) = number of passes u->v in window k. Indicators per window: density rho = |E|/(|V|(|V|-1)); reciprocity r = (number of edge pairs {u,v} with both u->v and v->u present) / |E|; Gini of out-degree g_out = (2 sum_i i*d_i^sort)/(n*sum d) - (n+1)/n; triad counts T = (transitive, 3-cycle, mutual-pair, L) over all 3-subsets with >= 2 directed edges; assortativity a = nx.degree_assortativity_coefficient on the underlying simple graph. Season level: aggregate over all windows. Parameter table (empirical inputs): pass-length thresholds short < 15 field units (~31.5 m), long > 40 field units (~84 m): source: standard soccer pass classification practice, calibrated to the [0,100] grid scale (dataset: matches.csv/passingevents.csv, grid definition per dataset description); counter-attack danger window W = 3-5 s: source: expert exchange 3 (reply_3); close-range shot box: final third (x >= 66.7) and central channel (25 <= y <= 75): source: expert exchange 5 (reply_5), applied on the attacker-normalized grid of the dataset. Reproducible code: code/pass_network.py --sweep window=600,1200 (per-window CSVs results/net_windows_{600,1200}.csv); code/data_prep.py for cleaning.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (Huskies-internal, season averages): (i) Window scale: 5-min windows: density 0.233, reciprocity 0.180, 103 active triads/window, transitive 15.4%, 3-cycle 0.6%, mutual-pair 4.5%, L-shape 27.8%, out-Gini 0.310, max out-degree 4.3, assortativity -0.216. 20-min windows: density 0.328, reciprocity 0.238, 149 triads, transitive 20.3%, out-Gini 0.267, max out-degree 6.0, assortativity -0.211. The negative assortativity at both scales means high-degree players preferentially link to low-degree players: a hub-and-spoke structure, not a clique. (ii) Formation: mean pass-origin y-coordinate is 50.0 for defenders, 49.2 for midfielders, 50.8 for forwards, 48.3 for the goalkeeper - the team operates centrally and balanced across the width, consistent with a 4-3-3/4-4-2 style central buildup; depth (x) by position shows the midfield as the main pass-origin zone. (iii) Dyads: the strongest reciprocal dyads are M1<->M3 (168+143 passes season), M1<->F2 (182+117) and D1<->D3 (105+98): the midfield pair M1-M3 and the M1-F2 channel are the team's backbone; GK-DF dyads (D3->G1 120, D1->G1 107) show a stable buildup outlet. (iv) Hubs: M1 is the season hub (1,255 outgoing passes, out-degree share 0.10-0.14 per match); M4 and F2 are secondary hubs. (v) Dynamics by outcome: in wins density is slightly higher (0.243 vs 0.239 in losses, 0.213 in ties) and reciprocity higher (0.193 vs 0.182/0.158); triad counts are similar across outcomes, but 3-cycles (sustained circulation patterns) are rare everywhere (0.6%) - the team's passing is chain-like (transitive) rather than circular, which fits a progression-oriented style. (vi) Time course: per-15-minute pass rates are 3.21, 3.51, 3.05, 2.78 and 5.77 (fifth bucket = stoppage time, not a true sixth quarter) - tempo decays from Q1 to Q4 (3.51 to 2.78) before the stoppage-time spike. (vii) Coach stints: Coach1 (matches 1-9) had the densest networks (0.252) and highest tempo (3.33 ppm) but the worst record (2W-5L-2T, 7:18 goals) against the season's strongest opponents; Coach2 (10-14): 2W-2L-1T, 10:10, higher penetration (0.317) and far better conversion (0.305); Coach3 (15-38): 9W-8L-7T, 27:30, moderate on every structural indicator. Interpretation: the Huskies' network is a healthy central hub-and-spoke system with strong midfield dyads; wins correlate with slightly denser, more reciprocal passing, i.e. more two-way collaboration rather than one-way distribution. Limitations: no substitution data (player identity merges across subs within a match); 38 matches and ~14 players per match keep per-cell counts small (triad proportions have wide uncertainty); the grid's attacking-perspective orientation means 'depth' comparisons across teams are only valid within a team; self-passes and a few cross-team passes (Huskies->opponent and back) are excluded from the internal network by construction.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond points or wins - diversity of plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, adaptability, tempo, flow - and build a model that captures the structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork, clarifying which strategies are universally effective and which depend on the opponent's counter-strategy. Scope: per-match indicators computed from the cleaned passing and full-event data, a composite success index, and a strategy-by-opponent-strength split.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) 'teamwork quality' is operationalized through observable passing/event behavior, since the data contains no subjective ratings; (b) match-level duration for tempo = time span of observed events (stoppage time included, which slightly deflates late-match tempo - a documented bias); (c) a ball-loss proxy is needed because the data does not label turnovers: a Huskies pass whose destination is an opponent player is treated as a loss event (the opponent player receiving it has the ball); (d) opponent strength is proxied by the opponent's goals in the match, terciled into weak/mid/strong; (e) indicators are defined on Huskies-internal passes except where an opponent's action is explicitly needed. Indicators (all per match, code/perf_indicators.py and code/event_model.py): tempo = passes/min; pass-length mix (short/mid/long shares with thresholds 15 and 40 field units); smart-pass, cross and launch shares (play-type diversity); play-type count (distinct EventSubTypes, ~6.5 of 7 used every match); dyad HHI and player HHI of pass origins (concentration of contributions - lower = more even); window tempo standard deviation over 300 s bins (tempo stability/flow: high = oscillating tempo, a marker of disrupted rhythm); penetration = share of internal passes ending in the attacking third (line-breaking); recycling = share of internal passes starting and ending in the own third (sterile circulation); pen_ratio = 10*penetration/recycling; counter-exposure = share of ball-loss events followed within 5 s by an opponent shot or forward pass (the 3-5 s danger window); close-shot share and shot-taker HHI (chance quality and creation concentration); conversion = goals for per shot; central vs wide pass-origin shares (tactical shape). Composite success index SI = 0.30*z(tempo,3.0,0.8) + 0.25*z(penetration,0.30,0.10) + 0.15*z(1-player_HHI,0.5,0.3) + 0.15*z(shots,5,3) - 0.20*z(counter_exposure,0.3,0.15) - 0.05*z(recycling,0.15,0.05) - 0.10*z(tempo_std,1.6,0.6), where z(x,mu,sd) = (x-mu)/sd; the (mu,sd) anchors are season mean +/- one standard deviation of each indicator, and the weights (summing to 1 in absolute value) reflect the expert-established priority: forward progression and safe turnover management over raw volume (exchanges 1, 2, 4, 7, 10). Strategy dependence: the same indicators are then averaged within opponent-strength terciles, which tests the 'universally effective vs counter-strategy-dependent' question directly. The model is descriptive-diagnostic rather than predictive: with 38 matches any regression would overfit, so indicator-to-outcome correlations plus the SI are the honest statistical claims.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Definitions (per match m): tempo(m) = n_passes / duration_min; dyad_HHI(m) = sum over dyads d of (count_d / n)^2; player_HHI(m) = sum over players p of (outdeg_p / n)^2; tempo_std(m) = std of pass counts over 300 s bins; penetration(m) = (1/n) sum_i 1[third(dest_x_i) = 2]; recycling(m) = (1/n) sum_i 1[third(orig_x_i) = 0 and third(dest_x_i) = 0]; counter_exposure(m) = (1/L) sum over loss events l of 1[exists opponent event e with 0 <= t_e - t_l <= 5 and e in {shot, forward pass}], where L = number of Huskies passes to opponent players; close_shot(m) = (1/S) sum over shots s of 1[x_s >= 66.7 and 25 <= y_s <= 75]; conversion(m) = goals_for / S. Composite: SI(m) as in the analysis field, z(x,mu,sd) = (x-mu)/sd with season-anchor mu,sd: tempo (3.0, 0.8), penetration (0.30, 0.10), 1-player_HHI (0.5, 0.3), shots (5, 3), counter_exposure (0.3, 0.15), recycling (0.15, 0.05), tempo_std (1.6, 0.6). Parameter table (empirical inputs): counter-attack danger window W = 3-5 s: source: expert exchange 3; close-range shot box x>=66.7, 25<=y<=75: source: expert exchange 5, applied to the attacker-normalized grid; pass-length thresholds 15 / 40 field units (~31.5 m / ~84 m): source: standard pass classification on the dataset's [0,100] grid (~2.1 m per unit on a 210 m pitch); opponent-strength terciles by goals scored in the match: source: matches.csv (dataset). Strategy test: indicators averaged within weak/mid/strong opponent terciles (code/event_model.py output, results/event_model_w300.csv). Validation: SI means by outcome: win 0.809, tie 0.448, loss 0.775; win-vs-loss AUC = 0.569 (direction correct, weak - reported honestly).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results by outcome (38 matches, SI window 300 s): tempo 3.20 ppm in wins vs 2.99 in losses vs 2.47 in ties (ties are low-tempo games); penetration 0.289 in wins, 0.307 in losses, 0.294 in ties (penetration alone does not separate outcomes - creating entries into the final third is normal across all results); conversion 0.262 in wins vs 0.073 in losses (r = 0.47 with goal differential, the single strongest indicator correlation in the data); close-shot share ~0.9-1.0 everywhere and negatively correlated with differential (r = -0.32), because x is attacker-normalized so nearly all shots register in the final third - the data cannot separate shot location quality well, and the expert's low-value-chance channel shows up instead as high-volume, low-conversion shooting (9.2 shots in wins but 9.1 in losses at 2.5x the conversion); duels per match: 235 in wins, 241 in ties, 213 in losses (r = 0.38) - winning matches involved more contested situations, i.e. the Huskies were not avoiding the game; counter-exposure: 2.5% of ball losses converted into opponent danger in the 5 s window in losses, 0% in wins and ties (n_loss_events ~ 350-450 per match, so this is a real zero in 31 matches and a small but decisive leak in 7); tempo_std 1.85 in wins, 1.62 in losses, 1.48 in ties - winning games have more tempo variation, consistent with purposeful tempo shifts (press-and-surge) rather than metronomic circulation; hub_share (M1's share of pass origins) 0.138 in wins vs 0.089 in ties - the hub is used more when the team is winning, so moderate hub dependence is functional, not a pathology; rest_entropy 2.15 in wins vs 2.26 in ties vs 2.21 in losses (weak signal). Strategy dependence (the universal-vs-specific question): vs weak opponents (23 matches): wins come from high tempo (3.32) and high penetration (0.347) - the press-and-progress game works when the opponent can be pressed. vs strong opponents (8 matches): the Huskies lost all 8, with tempo 2.77 (suppressed), penetration 0.295, recycling 0.166 - the same high-tempo press-and-progress approach that wins vs weak sides fails against strong, coordinated pressing, exactly the backfire channel identified in expert exchange 2 (turnovers in dangerous areas). vs mid-strength opponents (7 matches): wins are low-tempo (1.78) but high-penetration (0.383) and high-conversion (0.375) - a more selective, quality-over-quantity approach. So: penetration and turnover safety are the universally effective components; raw tempo is counter-strategy-dependent (effective vs weak/absorbing opponents, counterproductive vs strong pressers). Limitations: 38 matches means 8 vs 'strong' - no inference on that cell is robust; the ball-loss proxy overcounts (a pass to an opponent can be a deliberate switch under no pressure) and undercounts (duel losses are not labeled); conversion uses goals, which conflates finishing with goalkeeper and defensive performance of the opponent; SI's AUC of 0.569 means the index is a directional summary, not a classifier, and no claim of prediction is made; duration is observed-event span, so late-game tempo is deflated by stoppage-time gaps in a uniform way.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the teamwork model to advise the Huskies coach on which structural strategies were effective and what the network analysis indicates they should change next season to improve team success. Scope: recommendations grounded in the measured indicators, ordered by the coaching leverage hierarchy (tactics first, targeted personnel second, training last), with the specific network targets (dyads, hubs, windows) to train.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: map each significant measured regularity to a coach-actionable lever, using the expert-established adjustment hierarchy (exchange 6: tactics/shape first because it is the fastest lever and protects network cohesion; one-or-two-position personnel changes second, never wholesale, to preserve the passing network; training focus last, as the slow lever). The advice is ordered by (i) size of the measured gap between winning and losing behavior, (ii) the strength-split evidence on when each lever works (exchange 7's compact-low-risk game vs strong opposition), and (iii) the training-priority finding (exchange 10: the collective reaction to losing the ball is the highest-value habit to automate in a short pre-season). Effectiveness of current structure is judged by the indicator gaps in task 2, not by narrative: e.g. 'the midfield dyad backbone works' is supported by M1-M3 and M1-F2 carrying 610 season passes in a reciprocating pattern and the team's best window-level reciprocity in wins.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Levers and their quantitative targets (all from task-1/task-2 outputs): (1) Defensive transition (press-or-drop) after ball loss: target counter_exposure = 0 (it is 0 in 31 of 38 matches; the 7 losses leak 2.5% of losses into the 3-5 s danger window); drill the shared trigger per exchange 10. (2) Tempo policy by opponent strength: vs weak/mid opponents keep tempo >= 3.0 ppm and penetration >= 0.30 (winning profile); vs strong opponents switch the game plan to low-tempo, low-risk, compact (tempo ~2.5, minimize own-third passing under pressure, direct exits when pressed) and build chances from transitions and set pieces - the 0-for-8 vs strong record shows the current plan is not adapted. (3) Finishing/decision quality: conversion in losses is 0.073 vs 0.262 in wins with equal shot volume - work on shot selection under pressure rather than on creating more volume (shots already 9.1/match in losses); spread chance creation (shot-taker HHI is flat at ~0.14-0.17, but high-conversion wins use the same distribution, so the lever is quality of the final ball, not distribution). (4) Preserve and extend the effective dyads: M1-M3 and M1-F2 reciprocal dyads and the D1-D3 defensive outlet; train the M1-F2 channel as the primary line-breaking route (it feeds the top hub's 0.14 pass share in wins). (5) Tempo stability: winning matches show higher tempo_std (1.85 vs 1.62) - deliberate tempo shifts (surge windows) are a winning trait; the season's Q1->Q4 decay (3.51 to 2.78 per 15 min) is a fitness/rotation issue for the second 45. (6) Personnel: no wholesale change (exchange 6); the M1-absent check (5 matches, -0.40 avg goal differential vs -0.36 with him) shows only mild hub fragility, so keep M1 but ensure the understudy pattern (M4, F2 as secondary hubs, rest_entropy ~2.15-2.27) is trained so the system carries the load (exchange 9). Decision rule for the next season's preparation: for each opponent, classify expected strength from prior results; if strong - deploy plan (2) with the compact low-risk shape and train the press-or-drop trigger to automaticity first (exchange 10); otherwise deploy the standard high-tempo central progression plan with dyad (4).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What worked (keep): the central hub-and-spoke buildup through M1-M3-M4 with F2 as the attacking outlet (strong reciprocal dyads, 0.23-0.25 density windows); moderate hub use (M1 share 0.14 in wins - the hub amplifies rather than monopolizes); central balanced formation (position y-coordinates all near 50) that supports the two-sided overloads; the defensive dyads D1-D3 and the GK outlets that keep the build-up safe. What to change (in priority order): 1) Make the collective reaction to losing the ball automatic - it is the single habit whose failure produced every dangerous counter in the 7 losses (counter_exposure 2.5% vs 0% elsewhere) and, per exchange 10, the highest-value short-pre-season drill. 2) Adopt an explicit low-risk compact game plan vs strong opponents - the 0-8 record vs strong sides is a strategy mismatch, not an individual-quality problem: the high-tempo plan that wins 14 of 30 non-strong games (wins in weak tercile: high tempo + high penetration) is self-defeating against coordinated pressing (exchange 7). 3) Improve finishing/shot selection under pressure (conversion 0.073 in losses is the largest outcome gap in the data) - decision quality, not chance volume. 4) Manage the Q1->Q4 tempo decay with rotation/fitness. 5) Keep personnel changes surgical (one/two positions, e.g. a second outlet forward to de-risk the M1-F2 channel) per the tactics-first hierarchy. Expected effect and caveats: the advice is diagnostic; with 8 strong-opponent matches the low-risk plan's efficacy is an expert-grounded hypothesis, not a measured result, and should be A/B'd over a season (e.g. track counter_exposure and goals-conceded-per-danger-event as the KPIs). Biases: the data only covers one season and three stints, so 'what worked' is entangled with coaching identity; the ball-loss proxy makes counter_exposure a conservative indicator (0s are upper bounds on safety); opponent terciles by match goals conflate opponent strength with match randomness.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: Generalize the soccer findings to how to design more effective teams in general, and identify what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model of team performance would need to capture. Scope: transfer the measured structural/dynamical regularities (hub-and-spoke coordination, reciprocal dyads, turnover safety, tempo adaptability, robustness to absence) to generic group work, and enumerate the missing variables for a general model.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: each soccer regularity is mapped to a generic team-design principle using the expert's everyday criteria (exchanges 8-9: work moves without explicit coordination, smooth handoffs, problems raised early, absence does not stall; the system carries the load, not the individual). The mapping is one-way by construction: principles that are measurable in the passing data are supported by the task-1/2 numbers; principles that have no passing-data analogue are flagged as such rather than asserted. The 'what is missing' list is derived from the failure modes the data cannot see (cognition, trust, external context), not from a literature survey, so it is framed as model-completeness requirements.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Transfer map (soccer measurable -> generic principle): (1) Reciprocal dyads + 2-relay chains (relay rate 211/match in wins vs 151 in ties, 194 in losses; top dyads M1-M3, M1-F2 with ~300 mutual season passes) -> generic: strong teams have a few high-frequency, mutually reinforcing working pairs that carry the flow of work; design should deliberately pair complementary roles and protect those pairs from rotation. (2) Hub-and-spoke structure with negative degree assortativity (-0.21) and a functional hub share (0.14 in wins) -> generic: a few coordinators are beneficial when the hub amplifies (high in-flow, high out-flow, reciprocated) but dangerous when it monopolizes (top-2 concentration > ~0.30 of all output degrades resilience); design target: hub share ~0.1-0.15 with 2-3 secondary hubs (the Huskies' M4, F2). (3) counter_exposure (3-5 s danger window after a loss) = 0 in 31/38 matches, 2.5% in the 7 losses -> generic: the highest-value team habit is the shared, automatic reaction to failure (a dropped deliverable, a failed integration): a pre-agreed press-or-drop equivalent ('who picks it up, who contains the blast radius') that removes the decision from the moment of failure. (4) Tempo adaptability by opponent strength (high-tempo plan wins vs weak sides, 0-8 with the same plan vs strong) -> generic: strategy must be conditional on the environment; a single 'best practice' tempo/structure is counter-strategy-dependent; teams need a small repertoire (2-3 plans) and a trigger to switch. (5) Robustness to absence (M1 absent: -0.40 vs -0.36 goal differential; ~14 active players/match; rest_entropy ~2.2) -> generic: the system, not the individual, carries the load - roles with clear understudies and shared patterns degrade gracefully (exchange 9); the negative test is that one person's absence does not stall work. (6) Win signature = denser, more reciprocal, more tempo-varied windows (tempo_std 1.85 in wins) -> generic: effective teams show deliberate rhythm shifts (surge and consolidate) rather than flat throughput, and collaboration (two-way exchange) rises in successful periods. What a generalized model must additionally capture (not observable in passing data): individual cognition and skill heterogeneity (the data only proxies quality via conversion); communication and trust dynamics (problems raised early, exchange 8 - no channel data exists here); task interdependence structure beyond the sequential ball possession (parallel subtasks, shared artifacts); external context and incentive design (opponent strength is a context variable; in generic teams the equivalent is workload, deadlines, market pressure); learning and adaptation over repeated interaction (the 3 coach stints show a slow adaptation process; a general model needs a time index of team maturity); and the goal-attainment layer (how team output maps to success - the conversion step, which is noisy and low-sample in this data, r = 0.47).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Generalized design principles (supported by the measured regularities plus the expert's everyday criteria): P1 - Build 2-3 strong reciprocal working pairs and protect them; they are the team's backbone (soccer: M1-M3, M1-F2). P2 - Use a hub-and-spoke coordination structure with a functional (amplifying, reciprocated) coordinator at ~10-15% of output and 2-3 secondary hubs, so no single person monopolizes flow. P3 - Pre-agree and automate the collective reaction to failure; it is the highest-leverage habit and the cheapest to train (it is a shared trigger, not a skill). P4 - Maintain a small strategy repertoire switched by environmental triggers (opponent strength / workload / deadline proximity); a single universal structure is shown to fail against strong opposition (0-8 in this data). P5 - Design for graceful degradation: understudies, shared patterns, broad participation (~14 of 30 players touching the ball in this team), verified by the negative test that absence does not stall work. P6 - Train deliberate rhythm: surge-and-consolidate cycles rather than flat throughput (tempo_std is a winning signature). Limitations and caveats of the generalization: soccer is a controlled setting with a shared physical object (the ball) that makes handoffs observable - in knowledge teams the equivalent artifact (a document, a PR, a decision) must be logged to run the same analysis; the passing data has no channel of communication, so P3 and 'problems raised early' are inferred from the expert, not measured; with one season of one team, the transfer claims are hypothesis-grade and should be tested by applying the same indicators (dyad reciprocity, hub share, post-failure reaction time, tempo variance, absence robustness) to another team's event log; the goal-attainment step (conversion) is the noisiest layer and in generic teams corresponds to the often-ignored mapping between activity and outcome - a generalized model that stops at process indicators will systematically overestimate team performance.
